data.title: Erysipelas and cellulitis — viva
data.summary: Bacterial infections · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Erysipelas and cellulitis** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Difference between erysipelas and cellulitis?**
- Erysipelas: superficial dermis and lymphatics; raised, sharply demarcated, bright red, shiny plaque; mainly Streptococcus pyogenes; face and legs
- Cellulitis: deeper dermis and subcutis; ill-defined margins, not raised; S. pyogenes and S. aureus

**Q2. What is Milian's ear sign?**
- Ear involvement in erysipelas (dermis) — cellulitis spares the pinna because it lacks subcutaneous tissue

**Q3. Predisposing factors?**
- Breach of skin (tinea pedis/toe-web intertrigo — commonest portal), lymphoedema, venous insufficiency, obesity, diabetes, previous episodes, saphenous vein harvest, alcohol

**Q4. Differential diagnosis?**
- Deep vein thrombosis, stasis dermatitis (often bilateral — 'red legs' are rarely bilateral cellulitis), contact dermatitis, gout, necrotising fasciitis, erythema nodosum, panniculitis, herpes zoster (early), Wells syndrome, insect bite

**Q5. Red flags for necrotising fasciitis?**
- Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, woody induration, dusky/violaceous skin, bullae, crepitus, anaesthesia of skin, systemic toxicity, raised CK/LRINEC score — urgent surgical debridement

**Q6. Investigations?**
- Usually clinical; CBC, CRP, blood culture if systemic, ASO/anti-DNase B, swab of portal of entry; Doppler to exclude DVT; imaging if abscess/necrotising infection suspected

**Q7. Treatment?**
- Elevation, rest, analgesia, treat tinea pedis
- Oral penicillin V/amoxicillin (erysipelas) or cloxacillin/cephalexin (cellulitis) for 5–10 days; IV benzylpenicillin/ceftriaxone/cefazolin if severe; clindamycin or macrolide in allergy; add MRSA cover if purulent

**Q8. How to prevent recurrent cellulitis?**
- Treat toe-web intertrigo and lymphoedema (compression); prophylactic penicillin V 250 mg twice daily or benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks for ≥2 episodes/year

**Q9. Complications?**
- Lymphoedema (and vicious cycle of recurrence), abscess, necrotising fasciitis, septicaemia, glomerulonephritis, cavernous sinus thrombosis (facial)

## Quick spotter facts
- Sharply demarcated, raised, shiny red plaque on face crossing to ear — erysipelas

_Sources: DYP Survival Guide for PG Dermatology Exam (Bacterial infections — erysipelas, cellulitis); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch.15. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
